As an infosec professional, I feel the need to speak up here. This is not a defense of the practice, or the companies involved. It's merely some reality to go along with the hype.

1) Google and Apple are both developing APIs to allow for contact tracing. This is tech-speak that means they're providing the means for apps to perform contract tracing. You have to install an app that leverages the API for this to happen.

2) The contact tracing occurs using one of the low-energy wireless radios in your phone. A typical cellphone has multiple transceivers (radios) in it: A Bluetooth radio, an NFC radio, a WiFi radio, a GPS radio, a cellular radio, and even an AM/FM radio. Sometimes these are separate chips. Sometimes it's all one chip, and all the various functions are performed via software (this is known as software-defined radio). Most phones can only disable one or more of the radios via software (changing a setting on your phone). There is only one phone of which I'm aware that provides physical hardware switches to disable its radios.

3) Wifi, cellular, and GPS cannot be used for contact tracing. They are not accurate enough to determine what the powers that be have determined to be the "danger zone": within six feet of you. That's why contact tracing makes use of Bluetooth: it's powerful enough to reach six feet (things like NFC aren't), accurate enough (using the inverse square law) to determine if someone is within six feet of you, and doesn't require a bunch of hand-wavy fakery the other radios might (e.g., turning everyone's cellphone into a wifi access point and then attempting the same inverse-square-law measurement with 802.11 beacon frames). It also drains your battery less than such alternative techniques.

Be aware that, while wifi, cellular, and GPS cannot provide the accuracy necessary for contact tracing, they can place you in a fairly specific geographic area reliably. As just one of myriad examples, there are companies using this data to market to and/or propagandize to people who attended BLM protests. And they're doing it by determining who was there on the basis of data from wifi, cellular, and GPS, with the aid of a few cooperative apps, like Facebook.

4) Best practice for battery life, health, and security: If you're not actively using a radio, turn it off. Not using NFC? Disable it. Not currently using Bluetooth? Turn it off. Not actually connected to wifi right this minute? Turn it off. Don't need GPS right now? Off. And so on.

5) Don't trust what the OS tells you. As I mentioned above, almost every phone on the market allows the user to turn off one or more radios via software only. It's trivial to provide an interface to the user that lets them think they've turned something off, but in reality it's still on. Don't trust software. Get yourself a Faraday bag (whether an evidence bag, or something more convenient and easier to carry around, like a Blockit-Pocket bag, or similar) and when you're not actively using your phone, put it in the bag and keep it closed to block all EM radiation to/from your phone. You'll want to turn the radios off via software anyway, as things like wifi and cell radios that can't receive a signal use much more battery searching for a signal than they do when they've got one), but this will ensure your phone isn't giving off any unintended signals. Better yet, turn your phone off completely AND put it in a Faraday bag and close it.

This last statement may sound paranoid. But I've done this for more than 30 years. I've seen and done things that many people would think aren't possible with portable devices. Ways in which a phone can locate you and tell others where you are:

1) GPS. While a GPS receiver in a phone is just that, a receiver -- it does not transmit -- software and apps on your phone, including your web browser, can take the location information provided by the GPS receiver and transmit it to whoever wants it. GPS information can also be used to determine direction and speed of travel.

2) Wifi. Back in the late 1990s, wifi was in its infancy. No access points were secured, and there weren't that many around. Today, they're ubiquitous. Everyone has them, everyone's cable or DSL modems have them built in, they're provided in public spaces for convenience. As wifi began to gain in popularity, Google started doing something interesting: They started Google Maps. Interesting side note: Google Maps uses satellite imagery from old spy satellites it bought from the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). Specifically, Keyhole satellites. They also started building up something called Street View: They hired people to drive specially-equipped vehicles over almost all interstates, highways, and surface roads, taking photos so you can get a street-level view in Google Maps. They also, without fanfare, equipped these vehicles to collect information on every wifi access point they could detect, and their GPS location. Then, they used this information to determine with greater accuracy than GPS where you are. More precisely, where your phone is. By checking the wifi access points your phone can see, and their signal strength, against this database, they can triangulate your position with more accuracy than GPS alone. Nowadays, they don't do this with the Google Street View vehicles. They use your phones to do it: https://www.zdnet.com/article/how-google-and-everyone-else-gets-wi-fi-location-data/

Again, this data can be shared through the OS and apps with whoever wants it. Google and Apple both keep detailed historical records of everywhere you've ever taken your phone, complete with dates, times, and duration.

3) Elevation. Almost all phones now have altimeters installed. This tells the phone, and anyone who wants the information, exactly how high you are above sea level. So they can not only pinpoint your location on a 2D map; they can figure out, for example, what floor of a building you're in.

4) Acceleration. Just like the altimeters, almost all smartphones now have accelerometers installed. This provides information on whether the phone is moving or still, and how fast it's accelerating. So, for example, it can tell the difference between you walking down the street vs. driving, on the basis of acceleration rather than speed. It can distinguish between the phone falling vs. being thrown. It can tell how forcefully it's been put on a surface. And so forth.

5) Orientation. Almost all smartphones contain an electronic gyroscope and compass as well, which can determine with great accuracy which direction the phone is facing, and whether the phone is horizontal, vertical, tilted, etc. It can provide precise roll, pitch, and yaw data to whoever wants it.

And now, 6) relative position. Bluetooth is now being employed to determine the distance between your phone and other phones. Coupled with the built-in clock and GPS, and the other technologies I listed above, they can now know and share a) where you are (precise location including height), b) who you're near, c) what direction you're facing, d) how you're moving, e) your direction and speed of travel.

Smartphones these days also contain sensors to determine whether the screen is in contact or near-contact with your body, to determine whether the phone is in your pocket or against your head, vs. the screen being visible and away from your body. So they know and can share that information, too.

Now, think of the other sensors on the device, such as the microphone and cameras. Now think of the other information you consciously or unconsciously share every day, such as details about your life, activity, and locations on social media, timestamped, datestamped, geolocated, and often with photos.
